data.title: Chinese AI Tool Linked to Bank Hacks; Haze Shuts Schools in KL
data.description:
Artex, a Chinese AI cybersecurity tool, has stopped programmers from accessing its service after admitting it was misused by “bad actors” – as authorities in South Korea linked it to several recent bank hacks.

Artex was designed to help organisations strengthen their cyber defences through security testing to find potential weak points.

But the South Korean government said this week it was “highly likely” Artex had been used in data breaches at more than seven financial institutions, including major banks in recent weeks.

 

ALSO SEE: EU Envoy Warns China on ‘Unsustainable’ Trade Deficit; Oil up

 

Artificial intelligence’s ability to find previously unknown ways to hack into computer systems is in the global spotlight, as leading labs release increasingly advanced models.

Artex was “abused by some bad actors” to launch cyberattacks, the tool’s developer “Autumn-27” wrote on  Thursday on the code-hosting platform GitHub.

“Given the misuse of the tool, the Artex project will no longer be updated and will be converted to closed-source,” the developer said.

“No further versions will be released to the public, nor will maintenance support be provided.”

Artex had been open-source – allowing programmers to download its underlying code and customise it to suit their purposes.

Using Artex for cyberattacks was “entirely contrary to” the developer’s intentions, they added, without referring directly to the alleged South Korean cases.

South Korea’s Financial Services Commission says more than 68,000 people have been affected by the hacks.

Shinhan Bank, one of the breached institutions, said information attached to loan applications for about 25,000 customers had been leaked – including names, phone numbers and annual income.

 

‘Financially motivated’

In Japan, meanwhile, around 20 companies have said their data may have been compromised in a spate of similar cyberattacks, potentially impacting millions of customers.

The Japanese government has called on companies to strengthen their cyber defences.

“At this stage, it is not clear what the background to these cases is or whether there are any links between them”, Japan police chief Yoshinobu Kusunoki said on Thursday.

As AI makes hacking more sophisticated, “the scope of the damage is spreading across all areas on a scale that is difficult to compare with the past,” South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said on Tuesday.

US cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike said on Wednesday that its investigations into digital clues suggested the attacker had used Artex, and was potentially a 26-year-old based in China.

“The threat actor is likely a Chinese speaker and financially motivated,” a CrowdStrike blog post said.

Experts told AFP that Artex going closed-source would make the code harder for new users to obtain and adapt.

But the decision “cannot remove copies already downloaded or prevent people from continuing to use them”, said Poe Zhao, founder of the analysis publication Hello China Tech.

“Because the code was public, people could download it, change it and run it themselves. The developer could ask users to follow the rules, but had little control over their actions,” he added.

Ilya Kulyatin, CEO of Foundry Labs and founder of the Tokyo AI tech community, said users of open-source programmes can “remove restrictions built into the tool” which “makes certain forms of misuse easier”.

“But openness also benefits defenders: researchers can inspect the code, identify weaknesses and improve protection.”

 

China-EU trade understanding; Haze crisis

Meanwhile, top Chinese and EU commerce officials agreed on Friday to “strengthen” talks on trade, with Beijing saying it would facilitate the export of rare earths and magnets to the European Union, its commerce ministry said, citing a joint statement.

“Both sides reiterated the need to further strengthen the dialogue on export controls between China and the EU,” the statement said, adding “China is willing… to continue facilitating the approval of export licenses for rare earths and permanent magnets destined for the EU”.

The two sides reached an “understanding” on the trade of hybrid vehicles, Beijing’s commerce ministry said, citing a joint statement.

“After intensive consultations, the two sides reached an understanding on trade in hybrid vehicles in a manner consistent with World Trade Organization rules,” the statement said, noting both parties would “continue with the relevant procedures concerning company price undertakings”.

In other Asian news, Malaysia closed schools in Kuala Lumpur and other parts of the country on Friday, as haze from fires in neighbouring Indonesia again plunged local air quality to among the world’s worst.

Toxic smoke from peatland and forest fires has shrouded cities in the region for more than a month, sending respiratory complaints skyrocketing.

The school closures came as Malaysia’s leader discussed the choking smoke with his Indonesian counterpart and called for an urgent regional meeting.

Air quality in Kuala Lumpur has been at “unhealthy levels” this week, with a Swiss-based air quality monitor ranking the Malaysian capital among the world’s most polluted cities on most days.

Malaysia’s Education Minister Fadhlina Sidek said she has instructed school closures in four states and two federal territories, as well as a partial closure in central Pahang State.

Malaysia’s King Sultan Ibrahim weighed in on the matter on Thursday, saying schools should be closed as air quality readings reached 150 or higher on the Air Pollutant Index.

Under local guidelines, API readings above 100 are classified as unhealthy, above 200 as very unhealthy, above 300 as hazardous, while readings beyond 500 constitute the threshold for declaring a local emergency.

Kuala Lumpur on Friday showed a reading of around 170 API. The city was the second-most polluted globally behind neighbouring Singapore on Friday morning, Swiss-based air monitor IQAir said.

 

Anwar seeks help from Prabowo

Malaysia’s Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Thursday he discussed the fire situation with the Indonesian leader Prabowo Subianto.

“The haze issue is indeed at a worrying level. And I have personally contacted President Prabowo. And he also agreed to take the necessary steps,” Anwar said, without going into specific details.

He said Malaysia has been taking measures to combat the haze, including increasing attempts to trigger rain via cloud seeding.

Experts said the flames are being fanned by a turbo-charged El Nino weather phenomenon, causing the worst pollution conditions in years.

Anwar said he asked Malaysia’s Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan to contact the 11-nation ASEAN secretariat for an urgent meeting between environmental ministers to discuss the matter.

Singapore’s air quality levels too dipped into the “very unhealthy” range with a reading of 205 on the Air Quality Index, according to the IQAir website.

 

Stocks up, oil dips on US news

Stock markets climbed on Friday as oil prices dropped after President Donald Trump ruled out a strike on Iran before next month’s US midterm elections.

Trump said Washington was holding “productive discussions” with Tehran after reports that the White House asked the Pentagon to draw up plans for a possible attack ahead of the November 3 vote.

It was suggested that a show of strength might help struggling Republicans’ chances at the polls. That news caused the price of Brent crude to rise by over 5% on Thursday.

“The trajectory of the Middle East crisis remains highly uncertain, with Brent crude still trading around $103” per barrel despite Friday’s losses, noted Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club.

A separate major concern emerged over the technology sector. The Financial Times reported that OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, expected to make $50 billion in annualised revenue this year, below the $70 billion flagged.

That spooked tech stocks, although Bloomberg later cited unnamed sources as saying the firm expected to hit the original estimate.

Chris Weston at Pepperstone said “the discrepancy may reflect differences in revenue measurement rather than an outright deterioration in OpenAI’s underlying business”.

But, “in a market where valuations are increasingly dependent on ambitious revenue and cash flow projections, the headlines have been enough to trigger a meaningful one-day repositioning”, he said.

Wall Street’s Nasdaq ended down more than 1% on Thursday, with Nvidia down nearly 3%, while Microsoft, AMD and Amazon among others sharply lower.

But Asia mostly closed higher on Friday as early selling was pared back.

Europe’s main stock markets later posted solid gains in midday deals, while US futures traded higher.

Elsewhere, EU finance ministers struck a deal to create a new, more powerful European securities watchdog as part of the bloc’s efforts to unify financial markets.

The agreement announced in Luxembourg gives enhanced powers to the Paris-based European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), which will supervise major players.

Today it has only a coordinating role since national regulators supervise.

But the Frankfurt Stock Exchange operator Deutsche Boerse will be excluded from the body’s supervisory scope after Germany sought a carve-out, a diplomat told AFP.

data.title: EU Envoy Warns China on ‘Unsustainable’ Trade Deficit; Oil up
data.description:
The European Union’s top commerce official warned China on Thursday that the bloc’s trade deficit with China was “unsustainable.”

“Day one in China, with one goal: begin rebalancing our… unsustainable trade deficit,” Maros Sefcovic said on X, as he kicked off two days of talks in Beijing aimed at averting a trade war.

“I started by hearing directly from EU businesses here. The message around the table was clear: the need to improve access to the Chinese market, while boosting our economic security,” he added.

 

ALSO SEE: Climate Win: Australia’s Top Court Kills Big Coal Mine Expansion

 

Last year, every day, China exported to the EU around a billion euros ($1.1 billion) more in goods and services than went the other way, according to European figures.

Many in Europe blame this on unfair trade practices by Beijing, including state subsidies and price dumping, undercutting European rivals in industries from cars to chemicals.

They also fret over what they see as China’s manipulation of supply chains, as well as the devaluation of its currency.

Beijing has rejected those claims. The People’s Bank of China said on Thursday that “China’s trade development stems from the improvement of its industrial international competitiveness”.

“China has no need nor intention to gain trade competitive advantages through currency depreciation and will never engage in competitive currency devaluation,” the central bank said in a statement.

The problem for European officials, though, is they can ill afford to anger China. The Asian giant could throttle supplies of items such as rare earth minerals that are vital for the continent’s industrial sector – or throw up barriers to European exports to China.

 

Retaliatory trade weapon sought

The two days of discussions by Sefcovic in Beijing come as France and Germany, the bloc’s two biggest powers, threaten to up the ante.

According to a letter seen by AFP on Monday, President Emmanuel Macron and Chancellor Friedrich Merz called for a “credible instrument” to respond quickly to any escalation by Beijing, although China was not mentioned explicitly.

The proposed weapon – to be discussed at an EU leaders’ summit next week – would give the European Commission the power to respond to a trade aggression within days.

China immediately warned Paris and Berlin on Tuesday against “protectionist” measures.

“They should avoid going down the wrong path in the wrong way, only to ultimately suffer the consequences themselves,” the commerce ministry said in a statement.

China’s foreign ministry said on Thursday that Beijing hopes that it can work with Brussels “in the same direction and address each other’s concerns through dialogue and consultation”.

“As a principle, China has always believed that adhering to openness and cooperation and resolving economic and trade differences through equal dialogue and consultation is in the common interests of both China and the EU,” spokesperson Mao Ning said at a regular briefing.

 

Dependent on exports

The stakes are also high for President Xi Jinping, however, with China heavily reliant on exports in order to compensate for its stuttering domestic economy.

The EU parliament’s trade committee chief, Bernd Lange, said ahead of Sefcovic’s trip that this “economic crisis in China” gives the bloc “bargaining power”.

“The EU has a well-supplied toolbox to counter unfair subsidies, dumping, discriminatory procurement, and economic coercion. These instruments must be applied consistently and, where necessary, enhanced,” Lange said in a statement.

EU and Chinese officials have been negotiating since June, and Sefcovic raised hopes earlier this year when he said that he wanted “tangible results by October”.

Sefcovic has identified three priorities: addressing surging imports in strategically important sectors, increasing European exports to China, and improving access to critical raw materials.

The EU is also seeking clearer export-licensing arrangements for rare earths and other materials after China introduced restrictions last year.

Brussels hopes to manage Chinese exports through voluntary limits, for example, on hybrid cars shipped to the bloc. Beijing, though, firmly opposes import quotas.

Analysts are cautious about the prospects for a broad agreement being struck this week.

“But if one sector could be identified in which an export-restraint agreement with China could be tested, that would be a good step,” Ignacio Garcia Bercero, from Brussels think-tank Bruegel, told AFP.

Zhu Tian, economics professor at Shanghai’s China Europe International Business School, agreed, saying that the talks could yield agreements “on some specific issues”.

 

Oil soars 5% on talk of Iran strikes

Oil prices soared more than 5% on Thursday following reports that the United States could launch fresh attacks on Iran before next month’s midterm elections, risking further supply disruptions.

International benchmark Brent North Sea crude rallied to $105.46 per barrel and the main US contract, West Texas Intermediate, was up to $92.82 per barrel.

The Atlantic reported that the White House had asked the Pentagon to draw up options to hit sites in Iran ahead of the November 3 vote.

With Donald Trump’s Republicans in danger of losing both houses of Congress, an escalation in the US-Iran conflict risks even more pressure on the president, with Americans already battling record high diesel prices.

But the suggestion is that fresh US attacks could strengthen Trump’s position in seeking to bring Tehran to the negotiating table in a bid to end the war.

“The planning (for possible fresh strikes) should be seen in the context of efforts to pressure Iran, bring energy prices down, and demonstrate progress in the conflict ahead of the election,” noted Arne Lohmann Rasmussen, chief analyst at energy analysts Global Risk Management.

 

Shares down

The surge in oil prices weighed heavily on stock markets, with Europe’s main indices all falling in early afternoon deals, led by a 1.1% drop for Frankfurt.

Asia’s leading stock markets tracked losses on Wall Street, where technology firms pulled back from recent gains.

Shares in Samsung’s slid as the South Korean titan forecast a huge increase in quarterly profit but below market expectations.

On currency markets, the euro remains wedged at lows last seen in June 2025 on worries about France’s high debt levels, which have spooked bond markets.

Ahead of the Wall Street reopening, the Financial Times reported that Elon Musk’s SpaceX is aiming to raise $40 billion in bank loans and debt to further its purchases of AI chips from Nvidia.

The massive fundraising, coming just four months after SpaceX raised $86 billion in the world’s biggest IPO, underscored the voracious demand among tech firms for chips to roll out their ambitions surrounding artificial intelligence.

data.title: Climate Win: Australia’s Top Court Kills Big Coal Mine Expansion
data.description:
Australia’s most senior court ruled on Wednesday against a huge expansion of a coal mine several hours north of Sydney.

Three of the five judges in the High Court ruled that planning authorities must consider the emissions caused by burning fossil fuels, even if the coal is exported to other countries for use overseas.

The case involved the expansion of the Mount Pleasant mine in the Hunter Valley, an open-cut mine near the town of Muswellbrook, that local environmentalists have been battling since New South Wales planning authorities approved the expansion in 2022.

 

ALSO SEE: ‘Power Grid Inequity Hindering Asian States’ Shift to Renewables’

 

The verdict has been hailed as a landmark decision likely to be the first of many such rulings and the start of a slow process of shutting the door on coal mining and Australia’s prominent role as a coal exporter.

Australia was the source of more than a third of the world’s coal exports last year and the world’s biggest coal exporter by value, but it ranks second behind Indonesia in terms of export volume.

Those exports, from mines in all states but South Australia, generated $43.7 billion in 2025 for coal mining companies.

Local mining firm Mach Energy had sought permission to extend the life of the open-cut Mount Pleasant coal mine by more than 20 years until 2048.

Mach Energy argued that coal shipped off and burned overseas could not be clearly linked to environmental impacts felt in the Hunter Valley, north of Sydney.

But environmental campaigners disagreed, saying every ounce of greenhouse gas released into the atmosphere made bushfires, floods and drought more likely.

Campaigners were delighted by the verdict, saying the decision set a “binding national precedent” that required climate change damage to be considered when mulling fossil fuel projects.

Retired science teachers Wendy Wales and Tony Lonergan have fought for years to halt expansion of the Mt Pleasant mine, AFP reported.

“Today, the high court has said what we have always known,” Wales said. “We cannot dig up coal, ship it overseas, watch it drive climate change, and then pretend the consequences have nothing to do with us and won’t be felt by us.”

Lonergan said: “This isn’t the end of coal overnight. But it is the end of coal mine approvals that look the other way on climate.”

Wales and Lonergan first managed to halt the project in the lower courts of New South Wales. But Mach Energy appealed, eventually sending the case to the High Court in Canberra.

 

‘Historic ruling’

The High Court dismissed Mach’s appeal in a brief written judgment. It said the state’s planning commission failed to consider imposing conditions on the mine that would limit emissions “to the greatest extent practicable”.

Lawyer Anita O’Hart said it was a “historic” piece of environmental law. “The implications extend well beyond Mount Pleasant,” O’Hart, one of the lead lawyers in the case, said.

“This ruling will be applied by courts and planning authorities across Australia, and it will be studied internationally as one of the most significant domestic climate law decisions in the world.”

Mach Energy said it was “disappointed with the outcome” but accepted the court’s decision.

“We will continue to actively pursue all available options to ensure the long-term continuity of the Mount Pleasant operation,” the company said in a statement.

Australia’s coal mines have seen a boom in exports, because closure of the Strait of Hormuz has forced Asian countries to buy more coal as an alternative to disrupted gas supplies, analysts say.

That news comes at an awkward time, given the nation is preparing to champion clean energy as lead negotiator for the UN’s climate summit.

Instead of falling, as predicted by the International Energy Agency in December, global coal demand will rise 1.2% to a record 8.94 billion tonnes in 2026, the agency’s mid-year report forecast.

Australia is president of negotiations for the UN Conference of the Parties, or COP31, to be held in Turkey in November, where it will seek to highlight the peril of climate change to low-lying Pacific Islands, accelerate clean energy and mobilise investment.

Australia’s government said it has delivered Aus$3.9 billion ($2.7 billion) in climate finance from 2020 to 2025.

It is also shifting the population to renewable electricity, with a 2035 target to reduce emissions to 62-70% below 2005 levels. A third of households already use rooftop solar.

 

Pacific nations call for help

Pacific leaders pressed wealthy nations for more funds to help them “survive” climate change on Wednesday at a gathering aimed at drawing the world’s attention to life on the frontline of global warming.

This week’s “pre-COP” meetings in the Fijian city of Nadi are a precursor to COP31 in Turkey next month.

The South Pacific is among the regions most vulnerable to global warming – from rising seas jeopardising homes to increasing temperatures causing coral bleaching.

Speaking on the sidelines of the summit, Papua New Guinea Prime Minister James Marape told journalists it was an issue of “morality”.

“Nations who have sovereign borders are facing the threat of being nations no more,” he said. “We live with the burden of decisions made elsewhere.”

Pacific nations are using the pre-COP platform to push for more backing for the countries most affected by climate change.

The EU’s climate commissioner Wopke Hoekstra told journalists “we’re clearly not doing enough”.

A UN report released in August found developing countries needed $310 billion to $365 billion to adapt, yet had only $26 billion in adaptation finance available in 2023.

Regional leaders have set up the Pacific Resilience Facility with the hopes of raising $500 million, but it has so far brought in commitments for less than half of that.

Fiji on Wednesday announced an addition of $10 million for that fund. Fiji’s climate minister Lynda Tabuya told AFP one of her main messages to delegates in Nadi was the need to speed up the distribution of money for climate solutions.

“Part of our appeal going to COP is to make the current finance structure to be restructured so that it’s simplified,” she said.

“It’s frustrating. We are the least emitters in the Pacific, and yet we are the most disproportionately affected.”

Australian leaders also said it would invest US$2 million in regional road and communications infrastructure projects in Papua New Guinea, Fiji, Kiribati and Tuvalu.

 

Stocks dip, oil rises on Mideast flare-up

Oil prices rose on Wednesday on fresh concerns about Middle East supplies following a warning that Iran appeared to be stepping up attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, weighing on stock markets.

Crude futures had steadied on Tuesday, helping Wall Street to fresh highs, with a large amount of the support coming from a rush back into the AI trade that saw chip titan Nvidia push towards a $6-trillion market value.

“In Europe, where there is a lower representation of AI-related names, investors are taking a more cautious stance,” noted Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell.

“Oil prices remain above $100 a barrel and the inflation risks are clear to see,” he added.

Figures have shown Tehran increasing strikes on tankers in the crucial Strait of Hormuz.

UK Maritime Trade Operations on Tuesday said there had been nine attacks this month, representing half of the September total in the waterway and the Gulf combined.

But US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Wednesday that Iran has “lost complete control” of the Strait of Hormuz. “There’s almost as much oil flowing out now as there was before this conflict began,” he told reporters during a visit to Athens.

Chris Weston, head of research at broker Pepperstone, said “reports of increased flows across the (Mideast) region have offered some downside pressure on crude, but this has been offset by varying reports around the scale of attacks on vessels moving through the Strait”.

“For now, the market remains highly sensitive to headlines and geopolitical risk,” he added.

Meanwhile, Indian stocks slipped and the rupee steadied on Wednesday as the Indian central bank hiked interest rates for the first time in more than three years.

The euro fell heavily versus the dollar for a second time this week as worries about France’s high debt levels spook bond markets.

data.title: US Pushes AI Hotline With China, AI Heads Warn UNSC of Risks
data.description:
There have been positive developments in regard to global concern about the risks of artificial intelligence – plans for a special communication channel between the US and China, plus an important debate at the United Nations Security Council.

The United States has said it is looking to establish a dedicated communication channel on the issue, which was suggested during talks on the weekend between senior US officials and their Chinese counterparts ahead of President Donald Trump’s summit with Xi Jinping on Thursday.

“The US has proposed that we have a notification mechanism between the two countries” on AI, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said after his talks on Sunday with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng. The goal was to reach “a shared vision of common goals and common threats”, he said, without providing further details.

 

ALSO SEE: Big Oil Must Pay to Repair Damage Done to the Atmosphere: UN Chief

 

Trump has publicly dismissed concerns voiced by some in the AI sector that humanity could be wiped out by highly advanced AI systems within a decade if adequate safeguards are not put in place.

Fears have risen with reports that several models from Anthropic and OpenAI broke out of confined environments to access the internet.

Work towards “recursive super-intelligence”, where AI models build future versions of themselves in ways that humans may not be able to grasp, have sharpened the anxiety, as have moves towards AI controlling unmanned weapons.

The United States and China, engaged in competition for leadership in AI development, are reluctant to impose significant restrictions on domestic companies for fear of losing an advantage.

“We are seeing both sides starting to realise that there are possibilities of an incident occurring and of misuse, to the detriment of both countries,” said Jean-Marc Rickli, head of global and emerging risks at the Geneva Centre for Security.

He drew a parallel with the US proposal for a communication channel with China on AI and the Cold War “hot line”, which was established after the 1962 Cuban missile crisis.

AI has not yet triggered alarm on that scale. But Rickli noted a CNN report last week that said the United States military almost boarded a Chinese ship on the basis of an incorrect report drawn up using AI.

“If the United States and China … are going to safely navigate this brave new world, they will need the ability to communicate quickly and effectively about an emerging AI crisis,” said Lucy Luo, of the Washington-based Carnegie Endowment for International Peace think tank, AFP reported.

 

Superpowers’ differ on priorities

Yet the priorities and interests of the two superpowers are not always aligned.

A French researcher, Mathilde Viellet of the French Institute of International Relations (IFRI), noted that, since 2023, there has been a non-governmental dialogue between experts and research centres on the world’s most advanced AI models, including those from OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek and Alibaba. And there, both sides show “a difference in views on safety”, she said.

“The Chinese say that they have been working for several years on things such as deepfakes, information security, social disruption” while the Americans “are mostly worried about a loss of control and ‘misalignment’ of AI, when it acts in an autonomous way”.

The US consultancy Teneo said that “neither government is yet willing to commit to binding constraints on AI development”.

There is also the US preference for the development of proprietary AI models, owned by just one company, whereas China leans more towards open source models, for accelerated development and scale.

Rickli said the challenge, for Washington and Beijing, will be to find “the smallest common denominator”, which might involve coordination on crisis response or “possible ‘misuse’ by third actors”.

He said he believed “a hot line makes sense” in the military sphere, where AI is increasingly being used for targeting and accelerated decision-making.

IFRI’s Viellet said Washington and Beijing had a shared interest in discussing a loss of control of AI agents, plus its use by bad actors. They could reveal if models act in harmful or unexpected ways, divulge malicious use of AI or share information on evaluation of the safety of AI models, she said.

Altman has said agreement on shared standards testing would be “a wonderful achievement.”

 

<iframe width=”721″ height=”555″ src=”https://www.youtube.com/embed/qnLT-7vKYLE” title=”Full UN Security Council AI Hearing With Sam Altman, Dario Amodei and Clément Delangue | AC1G” frameborder=”0″ allow=”accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share” referrerpolicy=”strict-origin-when-cross-origin” allowfullscreen></iframe>

 

UNSC debate on AI risks

Meanwhile, the heads of leading AI companies warned the United Nations Security Council on Wednesday about the threat the increasingly powerful technology poses to humanity.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, plus Open AI chief Sam Altman, and Clement Delangue, the co-founder of Hugging Face, all spoke with the 15-member council. Amodei said he believed that if AI systems were poorly managed “AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole.”

“For all the differences of the people in this room, we must put aside those differences in order to confront this global opportunity and global threat that is being presented to us at the same time. No leader, no company and no nation can manage this alone,” said Amodei.

Hugging Face co-founder Clément Delangue highlighted the role of AI tools in defending against cyberattacks, citing an incident in which US giant OpenAI’s AI agents breached Hugging Face’s infrastructure after escaping their testing environment.

“We were attacked by AI, but more importantly, we defended ourselves with AI,” he told the council. He said Hugging Face relied on a Chinese AI model to help defend against the attack by OpenAI’s AI agents because it faced fewer restrictions than comparable US tools, according to Reuters.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman noted that international cooperation was needed.

But while the council met, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told reporters in New York that an AI agent developed by OpenAI infiltrated an Australian government website in June, accessing public and non-public files.

 

Trump welcomes Xi

Asian markets were mixed on Thursday as traders eyed a high-stakes summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping set to focus on AI, trade and the Middle East war.

Xi’s arrival in Washington coincided with US Treasury Scott Bessent announcing that the superpowers had agreed to extend a trade truce by two months.

The simmering trade war between the world’s top two economies is a key concern: while both sides have maintained a tariff truce for nearly a year, they have yet to secure a lasting agreement.

The “economic detente” will now extend beyond its November 10 deadline to January 10, Bessent said.

But hopes of business deals have been dimmed by the fact that there are no Chinese CEOs in Xi’s delegation, two sources told AFP. In contrast, top US tech bosses, including the leaders of major AI companies, are set to attend Thursday’s banquet.

“Market participants are looking for signs of cooperation (however feigned) in managing the risks of AI without raising the regulatory risk to the space,” said Kyle Rodda, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com.

 

Bond yields spike, trade truce extended

Hong Kong, Shanghai and Taipei were in the red, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi was closed for a holiday.

Japan’s Nikkei was 1.6% up as it reopened after a three-day break. Tokyo’s gains came as the benchmark 10-year JGB yield rose to 3.055%, hitting a 30 year high, after US bond yields jumped.

The benchmark US 10-year Treasury yield rose to 5.11% – its highest level since 2007.

The US Federal Reserve lifted borrowing costs last week, providing relief to traders concerned that policymakers were not moving quickly enough to address a spike in inflation.

The Iran war will be also on the agenda at US-China talks in Washington, Trump confirmed, despite having earlier played down reports that Beijing was supplying Tehran with intelligence as the conflict drags on.

Oil prices cooled off on Thursday after jumping sharply as world leaders at the UN General Assembly offered little to suggest progress in ending the turmoil in the Middle East.

The international benchmark, Brent crude, was down 1% in early Asian trade after soaring more than 3% the previous day.

Hopes for a deal to get Gulf oil and gas flowing freely through the Strait of Hormuz as global leaders gathered in New York had sent oil prices down in recent sessions.

On the simmering trade war sparked by Trump’s sweeping tariffs last year, US Treasury Scott Bessent announced Wednesday after intensive pre-summit talks that there had been an extension of a truce.

The “economic detente” will now extend beyond its November 10 deadline to January 10, Bessent said.

data.title: ‘Power Grid Inequity Hindering Asian States’ Shift to Renewables’
data.description:
Many Asian nations are lagging in the energy transition because of outdated power systems and rules that continue to favour the generation of fossil fuels, a large civil society organisation said this week.

South Korea and Japan have advanced economies and no shortage of resources for investment in grid infrastructure, but the two East Asian nations are among a handful of states accused of limiting fair access to their power grids.

That was the surprising revelation at a workshop given in Bangkok on Monday by Solutions For Our Climate, which examined energy integration, power grid access and market reform.

 

ALSO SEE: China National Day Travel Boom, Storm Over Starbucks in Xinjiang

 

Most Asian governments are accelerating electrification and expanding in renewable energy and bolstering their power grids, in a bid to meet increasing demand from AI data centres and other business sectors.

President Lee Jae Myung’s government in Seoul has a policy to create an ‘Energy Highway’ and expand renewables to more than 100 GW by 2030, however, there are concerns about such projects getting prompt access to the grid.

“In Chungcheong province, where half of South Korea’s coal fleet are located, offshore wind development is being pursued as part of efforts to replace the area’s aging coal fleet, but grid access is not expected to become available until at least 2032,” SFOC said in a statement.

“The case reflects a conflict of interests in South Korea’s power system – its state-owned utility Korea Electric Power Corporation (KEPCO) acts as a gatekeeper for grid access, creating bottlenecks for renewable energy.

“The problem is not simply whether countries can build more transmission infrastructure, but whether their power systems are shaped by the interests of fossil fuel incumbents.

“Reforms to biased grid access are urgently needed alongside investment in new transmission infrastructure in Asia. Furthermore, Asia should tackle the conflict of interests deeply rooted in the power sector in the longer term,” it said.

The workshop in Bangkok brought together civil society organisations from across the region to compare experiences and identify common barriers to renewable energy integration. Participants discussed underlying causes behind them and identified shared priorities to help map grid integration barriers within the region and opportunities for coordinated action.

Gahee Han, power market and grid head at Solutions for Our Climate, said: “It’s surprising to see that East Asia and Southeast Asia are sharing core issues – unequal grid access for renewable energy – leaving fossil-fuel generation protected while renewables face delays or curtailment.

“That is a question for countries across Asia, and countries must keep at the center of grid reform.”

 

Indonesia to halt forest destruction

In other Asian business news, Indonesia said on Tuesday it will halt a project to raze several million hectares of forest to clear land for rice production, as it had reached self-sufficiency levels of the staple grain.

The government launched a programme in 2024 to stop relying on rice imports within five years by clearing three million hectares of land for paddies, AFP reported.

Indonesia is one of the world’s most forested countries, and as such a major absorber of planet-warming carbon emissions from mankind’s burning of fossil fuel.

It aims to become a net carbon sink by 2030, with forests and other land use absorbing more carbon than they emit. However, observers have said continuing forest destruction for agriculture and logging, as well as rampant wildfires, could put Indonesia’s plans at risk.

President Prabowo Subianto hailed an “important victory” this year after data showed countrywide rice demand had been met with domestic production in one of the world’s top consumers of the commodity.

Climate envoy Hashim Djojohadikusumo said the government’s strategic reserve rice stock had reached about 5.3 million tons.

“The government sees no further need for expanding rice cultivation areas in the so-called forest areas,” said Hashim, who is Prabowo’s brother.

It was not known how much forest had already been replaced by rice paddies before the project was halted.

According to the National Food Agency, a government body that seeks to advance food security, Indonesia produced 34.71 million tonnes of rice in 2025 – over the annual demand of 31.19 million tonnes.

Haze from wildfires consuming forests and peatlands in Indonesia has blanketed neighbouring Malaysia and Singapore for weeks.

Hot, dry conditions associated with the El Nino weather phenomenon have fuelled the fires, which are also linked to land clearing.

 

Asian stocks mostly up

Asian stocks mostly rose on Tuesday as a tech-led record on Wall Street was tempered by ongoing worries about a spike in government borrowing costs.

Oil held most of the losses seen in response to a G7 release of stockpiles, Saudi Arabia’s price cut and a pick-up in Gulf exports to pre-war levels, though supply fears are keeping prices elevated.

The US Nasdaq closed at a fresh peak thanks to rallies in tech giants including Nvidia, SpaceX and Meta, though observers pointed out that the market gains were increasingly concentrated on a few stocks.

Asia struggled to match the positive energy on Wall Street in the morning but picked up as the day went on.

Tokyo, Hong Kong, Sydney, Singapore, Mumbai, Bangkok, Jakarta and Wellington also rallied, but Seoul and Manila edged down. Shanghai was closed for a holiday. London, Paris and Frankfurt were also on the up.

Still, there remains plenty of uncertainty among traders over the Middle East crisis, which has fanned energy costs and in turn pushed inflation higher – putting pressure on central banks to hike interest rates.

This has pushed government bond yields up to levels not seen for decades. Analysts say the race to build out AI data centres, servers and chips has compounded that problem, with tech titans no longer able to rely on their vast piles of cash.

Borrowing by firms including Google, Amazon and Microsoft hit around $500 billion in the nine months since January, and Goldman Sachs expects a further ramp-up in 2027, to $1.2 trillion.

“This is not something that we’ve seen before,” said Chris Della Fave, senior vice president at fundraising advisory firm Post Oak Group, who estimates that AI now accounts for 25% of all corporate bond issuance – up from 4% two years ago.

Oil prices sank to extend Monday’s drop, with Brent back below $100.

However, Saudi Aramco’s chief executive Amin Nasser, speaking after the G7 release, warned over global stockpiles.

“The system is already straining,” he told the Energy Intelligence Forum in London. “And with precious little else the world can turn to, the supply resilience cushion is scarily thin.”

Middle East oil exports, excluding Iran, surpassed their pre-war levels last week despite attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, according to data from the maritime tracking firm Kpler.

But FOREX.com’s Fiona Cincotta said: “Tensions in the Middle East remain elevated, with several vessels coming under attack around the coast of Oman and Yemen. This could limit the downside in oil prices, particularly if disruptions to shipping or regional supply intensify.

“The key question is whether improving crude supply can outweigh the geopolitical risk premium and keep oil prices under control. A sustained decline in energy prices would ease some of the inflation pressure currently complicating the outlook for central banks.”

data.title: China National Day Travel Boom, Storm Over Starbucks in Xinjiang
data.description:
Hundreds of millions of Chinese citizens celebrated the 77th anniversary of the People’s Republic on Thursday – by leaving town, via road, rail, or plane.

“Traffic demand is off the charts,” the state media outlet CGTN said, adding that international flights were up by more than 20% and that 2.1 billion trips were planned over the next week – about 300 million a day, according to the Ministry of Transport.

“October 1 alone could hit a record 340 million, nearly double the usual traffic,” it said. “Road travel, including self-driving, is expected to account for more than 90% of all trips, helped by free expressway access for vehicles of seven seats or fewer from October 1 to 7.”

 

ALSO SEE:  Investors Shaken by Global Sell-off of Government Bonds

 

Railways had “ramped up capacity,” with China Railway Beijing Group expecting to carry 22.3 million passenger trips over the 16-day holiday transport period from September 23 to October 8, with October 1 the busiest day at 1.79 million, it said.

Measures had also been introduced to boost tourist spending from late September till the end of October, with local governments planning over 20,000 events and providing more than 310 million yuan ($45.9 million) in vouchers and subsidies.

And there were firework displays in many cities, such as this one (below) in Hong Kong.

Inbound tourism is also growing, CGTN said. In the first half of this year, 22.9 million foreign visitors entered China, which was a rise of over 20% year-on-year.

 

Starbucks ‘morally bankrupt’

Meanwhile, an advocacy group and US lawmakers criticised Starbucks for opening its first cafes in Xinjiang, the autonomous region in the country’s west, where activists and foreign governments have alleged widespread rights abuses against the region’s Muslim Uyghur population.

The American coffee giant opened two stores in Urumqi, the regional capital, on Tuesday, in a move heralded by Chinese state media outlets.

John Moolenaar, chairman of the US House Select Committee on China, called the development “morally bankrupt” in a statement on Thursday.

The stores’ opening “ties an iconic American brand to the CCP’s brutal campaign against the Uyghurs” he said, referring to the governing Chinese Communist Party.

The World Uyghur Congress rights advocacy group said Starbucks “is once again choosing to ignore a dire human rights situation… by opening stores in the region”.

“Companies should not contribute to an economy where state-imposed forced labour remains a serious concern,” it added in a social media post.

The United Nations warned in 2022 of possible crimes against humanity in Xinjiang, including the detention of more than a million Uyghurs and other Muslim minorities in camps there. And rights groups say serious abuses continue in the region, including forced labour.

The Chinese government denies the accusations and says its policies have rooted out extremism and brought economic development.

The US has imposed sanctions in response to alleged abuses and several Western brands have faced criticism for connections to Xinjiang.

The Chinese government has invested heavily in Xinjiang – which was one of the country’s fastest-growing regions in 2025 – and is promoting a tourism boom.

Last year, Starbucks announced it would sell a controlling stake in its Chinese retail operations to investment firm Boya Capital in the hope of revitalising business in its second-largest market.

 

No consensus on overproduction at G20

In related news, G20 trade ministers are at an impasse on countering excess industrial capacity, top US trade official Jamieson Greer said on Thursday. That accusation is often levied at China, which rejects the criticism.

His comments came as trade ministers from the Group of 20 major economies met for a second day in the US city of Milwaukee. The United States holds the G20’s rotating presidency this year.

Ministers failed to find agreement on overcapacity, which is seen as a state subsidy that drives down prices unfairly, and on eliminating forced labour in supply chains, Greer said.

“Nearly all countries agreed that this is an issue that requires action,” Greer told a press conference, referring to excess capacity. He did not respond to questions on whether this was due to China’s objection.

“And nearly all countries agreed that our current system of trade remedies or responses is inadequate to solve this problem,” he said. He added that this justified unilateral US action.

There are US investigations into 16 economies on overcapacity, targeting China, the European Union, Japan, India and others.

Greer warned that countries which overproduce risk “creating an economy that rests on a house of cards.”

Trump also recently slapped tariffs on 60 trading partners over alleged forced labour concerns – another issue the G20 failed to reach agreement on.

 

‘Weaponization of food’

But G20 countries did find consensus against “the weaponization of food through coercive trade actions,” Greer said.

Temperatures rose over the issue at the two-day gathering as European officials criticized Russia’s attacks impacting Ukraine’s grain exports. Moscow and Kyiv have been locked in war since Russia’s 2022 invasion of its neighbour.

Russian and Ukrainian strikes targeting Black Sea ports have been wrecking and idling agricultural export capacity more quickly than trade flows can recover.

France’s minister delegate for international trade, Nicolas Forissier, told AFP on Thursday that European officials, including himself, and German and British representatives to the G20 criticized Russia over the matter.

“We have to say what we think, especially on the weaponization of food,” he said. European leaders’ comments against “the aggression of Russia in Ukraine” on food exports merely constitute “the truth.”

This did not mean the mood at G20 talks were bad, Forissier said: “On the contrary, I think the discussions are quite constructive.”

“There is a consensus on the fact that it’s not acceptable to weaponize food and agriculture,” he said.

 

Asian stocks fall

Meanwhile, Asian stocks dropped on Friday as investors grow increasingly concerned about surging oil prices and bond yields, while key jobs data later in the day will be pored over for an idea about the Federal Reserve’s next interest rate move.

Yields on US Treasuries and government debt in many other major economies spiked on Thursday amid fears that the surging cost of energy caused by the Middle East crisis will force central banks to ramp up borrowing costs well into next year.

And while they eased back early on Friday, angst continues to flow across trading floors, compounded by fresh worries of another flare-up in the US-Iran war.

Both main crude contracts edged up to extend the previous day’s rally with Washington and Tehran deadlocked on ending the crisis and unable to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Adding to unease, Axios said the US military was sending more warships, jets and troops to the region amid speculation US President Donald Trump could resume the war.

It said the USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier and its strike group could arrive in the Middle East next month.

Constantly high fuel costs have pushed up inflation since the start of the war at the end of February, fanning rate hike bets and pushing bond yields to levels not seen since the 2000s.

“Bond markets are now pricing in four further 25-basis-point rate hikes by June 2027,” FOREX.com’s Fawad Razaqzada said.

“That marks a dramatic shift in expectations from before the US-Iran war at the start of the year, when markets were anticipating at least 100 basis points of rate cuts over the same period.”

He pointed out that the Bloomberg Commodity Index had jumped more than 37% on-year and was set for one of its largest 12-month gains since the 2022 energy crisis.

“The scale of the advance points to a renewed wave of commodity-driven inflation, complicating the outlook for central banks as borrowing costs continue to rise,” he warned.

A positive lead from Wall Street was unable to provide any support to Asian stock markets, with Hong Kong losing more than 2% and Tokyo, Singapore, Wellington, Manila and Jakarta also down. Shanghai is closed for a holiday.

Seoul, however, was supported by another jump in chipmakers SK Hynix and Samsung, while Sydney and Taipei were up, too.

US non-farm payrolls figures later Friday are in focus as traders try to ascertain the Fed’s next move after last month’s rate hike.

A below-forecast read on the bank’s preferred measure of inflation this week helped ease concerns for a second successive lift on October 28, but a strong jobs read could strengthen the case for such a move.

Optimism for a hold has been given a shot in the arm this week by some officials calling for a measured approach.

data.title: Investors Shaken by Global Sell-off of Government Bonds
data.description:
On the first day of the last quarter of 2026, investors were showing signs of doubt about rising levels of government debt, despite indications that the tech and AI boom is far from over.

European stocks slid on Thursday amid mounting concern about high and rising government debt levels, with heavy selling of the benchmark 10-year US Treasury note sending its yield to the highest level since the dot-com bust in 2002.

Amid the global sell-off in government bonds, French and UK 10-year yields also struck their highest levels since the 2000s, while 30-year bonds also hit multi-decade peaks on growing inflation fears.

 

ALSO SEE: China Opens Joint Airbase in Laos, Extends Probe Into US Trade

 

“It looks like the relentless rout in the bond market is sending investors running for cover,” said Neil Wilson, a market strategist at Saxo UK.

The US 10-year yield hit as much as 5.34%, with renewed advances for oil prices adding to the inflation fears as Brent crude once again surpassed $100 a barrel.

 

Strong gains on Nikkei, Kospi

The technology sector was in rude health, however, helping the Tokyo and Seoul stock markets to close with strong gains despite growing worries over AI safety.

Google said on Wednesday that it would initially withhold its most powerful artificial intelligence model from the public, releasing Gemini 4 Argon only to a vetted group of cybersecurity experts to avoid misuse by hackers.

The cautious rollout mirrors the approach of rival Anthropic, which has kept its most advanced model, Claude Mythos Preview, restricted to a small number of trusted organisations.

Wall Street stocks finished mixed on Wednesday as support for tech stocks and well-received US economic data was offset by the lofty bond yields.

“Asian stocks with links to AI still managed strong gains as they reacted to a blockbuster set of earnings from US memory chip outfit Micron,” AJ Bell investment director Russ Mould was quoted as saying by AFP.

“US futures pointed to a higher open on Wall Street later, largely thanks to this artificial intelligence-related boost,” he added.

Chipmaker Micron Technology provided a much-needed boost to investors amid lingering worries about the vast sums pumped into the AI sector in recent years, and when companies will see returns.

Traders are meanwhile awaiting Friday’s US jobs data for clues on whether the Federal Reserve will follow up last month’s interest rate hike, aimed at combatting elevated inflation, with another round of tightening in October.

The prospect of back-to-back increases eased on Wednesday after the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge came in at 3.4% year-on-year in August, unchanged from July.

Separate official US data showed a large upgrade to economic growth in the world’s biggest economy during the second quarter, to 2.2%.

 

No decision on Alaska gas: Seoul

In Asian business news, South Korea said it has agreed to invest billions of dollars in US energy projects, but expressed regret on Thursday that the US announcement of their dealings “went beyond what had been agreed upon.”

Seoul had previously agreed to invest $350 billion in the United States and increase purchases of American energy under a July 2025 trade deal that set 15% tariffs on imports from the East Asian nation.

US President Donald Trump announced on Wednesday that $200 billion in South Korean energy investments, including $54 billion for a liquified natural gas (LNG) project in Alaska.

“The United States and Korea have agreed to commence working together on the 50 Billion Dollar ALASKA LNG PROJECT,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social account.

While Seoul has confirmed some planned investments, its trade ministry said in a statement that “no decision has been made whether to invest” in the Alaska project, including the “scale of any potential investment” in it.

“South Korea and the US share the understanding that the Alaska project will not proceed unless it is commercially viable,” trade minister Kim Jung-kwan told a briefing.

“I expressed regret to US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over the remarks that went beyond what had been agreed upon,” he added.

The trade ministry confirmed that both sides intended to “proceed with a $22.3 billion natural gas power facility” in Texas, dedicated to “supplying power to co-located data centers.”

Trump in his post said that the “huge 22 Billion Dollar, 6.4-gigawatt Natural Gas Fired Power Project in Encinal, Texas… will bring tremendous new, reliable Power Capacity to Texas.”

The facility will provide 6,472 MW of energy to data centers also located in Encinal, a US Commerce Department statement said. It is expected to come fully online by 2032.

 

8 nuclear reactors

President Lee Jae Myung also said on Thursday that Seoul would begin working on the Alaska project on the “condition that 1) its commercial viability is confirmed and 2) it complies with South Korea’s legal procedures.”

Lee said last month that negotiations had been “very complex and difficult” and that he had found some terms “difficult to accept,” without elaborating further.

Beyond the Alaska and Texas projects, Trump said the two countries were “moving forward” with a $120 billion nuclear power program to build eight large-scale reactors in the United States.

The figure includes $100 billion for construction costs and $20 billion in contingency reserves, the US Commerce Department said.

Lee said Thursday that the nuclear power project would likewise depend on the “commercial viability” of each individual reactor.

The US projects will be “pursued in a manner that serves the national interest,” South Korea’s trade ministry said.

The Alaska project, led by New York- and Houston-based developer Glenfarne Group, envisions an 800-mile (1,300-kilometre) pipeline carrying North Slope gas to a liquefaction facility near Anchorage for export to Asia.

While Alaska has decades of history as a petroleum producer, environmental concerns have historically constrained some developments.

But the Trump administration has largely brushed aside those concerns, canceling regulations to reduce emissions that are blamed for global warming.

Trump’s industrial ramp-up envisioned for his widespread energy projects faces a potential labour shortfall, experts say.

The United States needs to fill an estimated 1.7 million skilled trade openings through 2035, according to a report released on Wednesday by the Alliance for America’s Skilled Trades, an organization of Ford, Blackstone, Nvidia and other large companies.

The report found today’s training programs produce just 55 workers for every 100 needed.

‘Plastics treaty possible’

Meanwhile, there was more positive news from Bangkok. Countries negotiating a world-first treaty to limit plastic pollution are less divided than before and a deal could be agreed in March, the diplomat chairing the talks told AFP on Thursday.

Chilean ambassador Julio Cordano took over the role earlier this year after his predecessor resigned, and with the talks having overrun their initial schedule by more than a year.

But speaking in Bangkok after informal closed-door talks with heads of delegations, Cordano said he was hopeful a deal could be clinched at the next official round of negotiations.

“My plan and my expectation is that we will be able to adopt the treaty in INC 5.4 (March meeting), if we follow the correct steps, if we make consistent progress, and if we complete the roadmap that I presented,” he said.

Work on a treaty to address plastic pollution began in 2022 with a two-year timeline. But crunch talks in South Korea in 2024 fell apart, and a renewed effort in Geneva the following year made no progress either.

A majority of nations have called for ambitious, legally binding measures to curb production of plastic, which is expected to triple by 2060.

But a smaller bloc of mostly oil-producing states – including Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Russia – have pushed back against such restrictions, seeking to focus more narrowly on waste management.

Ahead of the Bangkok talks, Cordano released an “aid to negotiations” – a non-binding outline of a possible treaty, with brackets around the most contentious sections.

These are mostly the same issues that sank previous rounds, including a cap on plastic production, mention of human health, and designating problematic plastic products or chemicals of concern.

But Cordano insisted countries were not as far apart as they might seem.

“I think you would be surprised to hear members on these topics. I think they are much more closer than simply binary positions that are irreconcilable,” he said.

 

‘Different pathways’

Sources told AFP some countries are increasingly supportive of a document that would offer options, with more ambitious countries choosing to limit production or certain products, while others do not.

Cordano said the idea of “different pathways or different departure points” was “embedded in our mandate.”

He also called for pragmatism and a focus on the end goal of a treaty.

“There’s more than one way to achieve that, and I think members are realising that.”

There are still serious disputes to resolve, however, including mechanisms for adopting a treaty and amending it in the future.

Some countries want all decisions to be made by consensus, which opponents say allows a small minority to block progress.

Cordano said his goal remained a “treaty that will be accepted by everyone,” but he acknowledged concerns about future application of a deal if consensus is the rule.

It is “about how can we collectively understand and come up with a system that would allow this treaty in the future to be effective, not to be stopped, not to be frozen because there is no consensus,” he said.

The diplomat expects to release a new “aid to negotiations next month, before a last round of informal talks in January.

“Everybody sees that this is a problem that requires a solution,” he said. “I think people are seeing eye-to-eye… I think this is a reason to be optimistic.”

 

Asian tech firms stand out

Meanwhile, technology firms led gains on a mixed day for Asian stocks on Thursday as traders welcomed positive earnings from chip giant Micron.

However, concerns about elevated government bond yields and spiking oil prices tempered the optimism, even after a batch of healthy US economic data.

Tokyo and Seoul were the standout markets as chip makers and other leading tech companies rallied after Micron CEO Sanjay Mehrotra announced “record fiscal 2026 results, and we expect an even stronger fiscal 2027”.

The news provided a much-needed boost to investors amid lingering worries over the vast sums pumped into the AI sector in recent years, and when – if at all – they will see returns.

“Micron is locking in more of tomorrow’s demand through long-dated customer agreements at the same time it is committing huge sums of capital to build the capacity needed to meet it,” wrote Stephen Innes at SPI Asset Management.

Tokyo’s Nikkei ended up more than 3%, with Advantest up almost 10% higher, Tokyo Electron adding more than 6% and investor SoftBank more than 5%.

However, Nidec stocks plunged almost 20% at one point after the world’s leading manufacturer of small precision electric motors reported a massive impairment loss following a prolonged accounting crisis. It halved its losses by the end of the day.

In Seoul, the Kospi jumped 2% as chip titan SK Hynix added 3.2% and Samsung piled on 2.8%, while Taipei was lifted by a 1.2% advance for TSMC.

There were also gains in Singapore and Bangkok, though Sydney, Wellington, Manila, Mumbai and Jakarta fell.

Hong Kong and Shanghai were closed for holidays.

data.title: Australian Rates Hit 15 Year High, Asian Stocks Fall, Oil Up
data.description:
Australia’s central bank lifted interest rates on Tuesday to their highest level in 15 years.

The board of the Reserve Bank made a unanimous decision to raise rates by 0.25%, lifting the cash rate target to 4.6%, the highest since 2011, to counter inflation that the government says was spurred mainly by the oil crisis in the Middle East.

In Southeast Asia, the United Nations warned Malaysia that forcibly returning thousands of refugees and migrants back to Myanmar – a country divided by a severe civil war for the past five and half years – could impose severe risks to those being returned.

 

ALSO SEE: TikTok Settles Child Safety Trial; Meagre US-China Trade Deal

 

And in Bangkok, airport and Thai Airways officials apologised for delays in flights and baggage handling, caused partly by flooding in the capital that prevented staff from commuting normally.

Meanwhile, stocks on Asian markets mostly fell, and oil prices extended gains, as hopes for a reopening of the Strait of Hormuz fade, amid expectations the US Federal Reserve will hike interest rates again next month.

Hopes for an easing of Middle East tensions were dashed at the weekend when Donald Trump rejected Iran’s offer for a seven-day truce.

Trump said talks would resume this week, but that was unable to lift the gloom on market floors, with traders contemplating further rises in inflation that will force the Fed to tighten monetary policy more.

 

Trump denies offering sanctions relief

The US president on Monday denied a report by the news outlet Axios that he offered Iran sanctions relief and the release of frozen funds, as the Middle East war drags on.

“Axios just released a story that ‘Trump’ offered Sanctions Relief and Frozen Funds to Iran. This is untrue. I offered them NOTHING!,” Trump said on his Truth Social platform.

The story, quoting unidentified US officials, said Trump “is willing to give Iran sanctions relief and release Iranian frozen funds in return for concrete Iranian steps regarding the nuclear program”.

The 80-year-old Republican called the story “a HOAX” and said the news site should withdraw it.

However, Iran’s state broadcaster said the country’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, will meet Qatari representatives, AFP reported.

The talks are expected to focus on “messages exchanged with the United States through intermediaries… particularly regarding the conditions set by Iran for the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz”.

Tehran officials have privately expressed pessimism about making a deal to reopen Hormuz before November’s US midterm elections, Bloomberg reported sources as saying.

The waterway is key to the world’s oil and gas deliveries and is now central to the US-Iran conflict, particularly with the Iran-backed Houthis seizing Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast, including the Bab al-Mandab Strait, another vital shipping lane.

“Our expectations remain that the conflict will be with markets for the foreseeable future and the global economy will continue adjusting to the realities of the supply disruptions,” said Ian Lyngen at BMO Capital Markets.

 

Gold falls on rate hike bets

Both main crude contracts rose more than 1% on Tuesday, and the lack of any progress in ending the conflict continues to put upward pressure on fuel costs.

Average UK diesel prices have hit a record high, according to the RAC motoring organisation.

Equity markets struggled following a day in the red for all three main indexes on Wall Street.

Markets in Tokyo, Seoul, Hong Kong, Mumbai, Singapore, Taipei, Wellington, Jakarta and Manila were all down, but Shanghai and Sydney rose.

London, Paris and Frankfurt also rose.

Gold held Monday’s steep losses to sit around $4,140 as traders bet on more rate hikes, which makes the non-interest-bearing metal less attractive.

Investors are also gearing up for the release of key US inflation and jobs data this week that could play a role in the Fed’s decision-making, with markets pricing in a second successive rate hike at the end of October.

“The main concern for markets isn’t that employment conditions could suddenly weaken. It’s almost the opposite,” wrote Fiona Cincotta at FOREX.com.

“Economic data has remained surprisingly strong despite higher rates and energy prices,” she added.

“Typically, stronger non-farm payrolls (jobs) are positive for stocks, but that is not necessarily the case when inflation is also rising sharply.

“Strong employment could instead strengthen the case for the Fed to keep rates higher for longer, or even hike rates again to bring inflation under control.”

In company news, fast-fashion giant Shein fell almost 14% at one point in Hong Kong after releasing disappointing earnings.

It was the firm’s first report since listing at the start of the month following a high-profile $1.7 billion initial public offering.

data.title: TikTok Trial Set to Start in US, Xi Could Meet Trump Again
data.description:
TikTok faces court hearing in the US on Monday for allegedly misleading parents about tools meant to shield children from harmful content.

The trial in a state court in Montgomery, Indiana, is the first case against the platform to go before a US jury.

The case, which is expected to last two to three weeks, comes as social media companies face a wave of litigation across the United States over the harm their apps allegedly cause young users.

 

ALSO SEE: US Pushes AI Hotline With China, AI Heads Warn UNSC of Risks

 

TikTok has until now settled cases against it that were headed for trial, including a Los Angeles lawsuit brought by a young woman and a suit from a Kentucky school district.

Meta, by contrast, has taken its chances in court – with bruising results.

In March, a jury in New Mexico ordered the Facebook and Instagram owner to pay $375 million after finding it had misled the public about the safety of its platforms for children.

That same month, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and Google’s YouTube negligent in the case of a 20-year-old woman who said she became hooked on social media as a child, awarding her $6 million.

In August, Meta agreed to pay $18 billion to settle a sweeping lawsuit brought by US states accusing it of designing Instagram and Facebook to addict children.

‘Engineered to hook young users’

Going to trial could expose TikTok to unprecedented public scrutiny of how it handles safety internally, with company documents and executive testimony potentially aired in open court.

Alabama originally sued TikTok and its Chinese parent company ByteDance in April 2025, alleging the app was engineered to hook young users “just like a sophisticated gambling machine.”

The state later narrowed its case to claims under Alabama’s Deceptive Trade Practices Act, focusing on whether TikTok misrepresented the effectiveness of features such as “Restricted Mode” and “Kids Mode.”

In its complaint, the state said investigators set up TikTok accounts posing as 13-, 14- and 15-year-olds in Alabama and switched on Restricted Mode.

Despite TikTok’s assurances that users in that mode should not see mature themes, the accounts were quickly served videos about suicide, self-harm, eating disorders, alcohol and sex, according to the filing.

The state also accuses TikTok of falsely telling app stores the platform was suitable for children aged 12 and up and contained only mild or infrequent mature content.

TikTok, whose US operations were transferred this year to a venture led by American investors, has argued that the case should be paused and that it is shielded by Section 230, a federal law that protects online platforms from liability for content posted by users.

The company has said it “designed its platform with teen safety as a key priority.”

Alabama is seeking an injunction for TikTok to change its practices, civil penalties and damages.

 

Xi says ‘We could meet again’

Meanwhile, Chinese President Xi Jinping floated the possibility of two more meetings with US President Donald Trump this year, as he wrapped up a state visit to Washington on Friday.

“Looking ahead to the remainder of this year, there will be two more opportunities for us to meet each other – firstly the APEC meeting in China and then the G20 summit in the United States,” Xi, speaking through a translator, said as he had tea with Trump at the White House.

“I do welcome you, Mr President and the First Lady, to visit China.”

Analysts have suggested that President Xi is keen for his US counterpart to scrap an arms deal for Taiwan.

President Donald Trump, meanwhile, said on Friday that he and Xi Jinping had made progress for the United States and China, as the Chinese leader wrapped up a state visit to Washington.

“I think we’ve made tremendous strides, we’ve made great strides, very positive for both countries,” Trump told reporters as he and his wife Melania had tea at the White House with Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan.

Details of the latest US-China trade negotiations are due to be released on Monday, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said.

 

Oil dips on Iran offer

In other business news, oil prices slid on Friday on reports of potential overtures to end the US-Iran war, which helped support stock prices after a volatile week as investors tracked geopolitical tensions.

Wall Street indices opened higher following slight gains in Europe and a mixed performance in Asia, against a backdrop of rising government bond yields and persistent inflation fears.

After falling sharply on hopes of a breakthrough to end the Middle East war during the UN General Assembly in New York this week, oil prices jumped when there was no sign of tangible progress.

But they fell back on Friday after Iran’s foreign minister said it had submitted an offer to Washington that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz to tanker traffic within seven days.

“If certain conditions are met, the strait will be open within seven days and talks will start,” Abbas Araghchi told media outlets on the sidelines of the UN gathering.

“It is a dubious offer considering Iran hasn’t changed its conditions from before,” said Patrick O’Hare, an analyst at Briefing.com. “We’ll see how long the glow of Iran’s offer lasts.”

Inflation fears from the Strait of Hormuz closure, alongside the risk of further Gulf supply cuts due to Houthi strikes on Saudi infrastructure on the Red Sea, have again pushed up government bond yields, with investors demanding higher returns for lending money.

The benchmark US 10-year Treasury yield hit its highest level since 2007 on Thursday, and Japan’s government bond yields also hit multi-year highs.

Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey hinted meanwhile that it could also follow the European Central Bank and US Federal Reserve in hiking interest rates in the coming months, which could curtail inflation but slow economic growth.

As for equities, “a seemingly amicable meeting” between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping in Washington helped lift investor sentiment, said Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell.

However, the nations’ extension of a trade truce by two months until January was far less than the two years the Chinese had hoped for.

“US-China trade risks remain… (with) issues over tariffs, agricultural purchases, rare earths, and technology restrictions unresolved,” said MUFG market strategist Lloyd Chan.
